title: The firebrand
hookLine: a torch from a funeral pyre is useless; four kinds of people

cards: In ancient India the dead were burned on open pyres at the edge of town. When the fire went down, what was left was ash, bone and charred sticks.
Picture one of those sticks, burning at both ends and smeared with dung in the middle. Nobody would carry it home for the kitchen fire, or take it into the forest to build with.
It's good for nothing, in the village or out of it. The Buddha picks up exactly that stick, in words, and holds it up to a room of monks.

teach.b: The sutta, in the Book of Fours, sorts people into four kinds. The first practices neither for their own good nor for the good of others.

teach.h: THE FIREBRAND: NO USE AT ALL.
OWN GOOD ABOVE OTHERS' GOOD ALONE.
teach.b: The second practices for the good of others, but not their own. The third, for their own good, but not for others. The fourth, for both.
Look at the middle two. The Buddha puts the one who works on themselves above the one who works only for others.

That can sound selfish, until you see what 'own good' means here: taming greed, hatred and confusion in yourself. Someone who rushes to fix everyone else while their own temper is on fire can make a lot of smoke.

The texts elsewhere give a picture: you can't pull someone out of a swamp while you're sinking in it yourself. But the sutta doesn't stop at self. The highest of the four is the one who practices for both.
Then a dairy image. From a cow comes milk, from milk curd, from curd butter, from butter ghee, and from ghee the cream of ghee, the finest of all.

teach.h: THE BEST: FOR SELF AND OTHERS.
teach.b: That cream is the person who works for self and others together. Not first one, then the other: both, in the same life, in the same day.

how: Many Buddhist teachers describe practice as having two sides, working on one's own mind and serving others, and the firebrand sutta is one of the early texts they cite for holding the two together.

o: a stick from a pyre, useful to no one
a torch carried to light the way home
a fiery speaker who stirs up a crowd

s: the sutta ranks working for others alone as the highest
highest is the one who works for both self and others.
the firebrand is useless in the village and in the forest
it can't be carried home as fuel or used as timber.
the sutta ends with milk, curd, butter, ghee and cream of ghee
the cream of ghee stands for the person who practices for both.

games.q: of the four kinds of people, which does the Buddha call the highest?
o: the one who works only for others.
the one who works for self and others.
the one who works only on themselves.
games.why: the one who practices for both. surprisingly, the sutta puts working on yourself above working only for others, but it ranks both together above everything.

practice: Notice one thing in you that's smoking right now, a worry, an irritation, and breathe with it gently until it cools a little.
Then bring to mind one person who could use a small, real help: a message, a dish washed, a question asked and listened to. Breathe in for yourself, and breathe out for them.

wordCard.voice: The firebrand. In the Numbered Sayings, the stick from a funeral pyre that's useless everywhere: the picture of a life lived for no one's good. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali chavalata: a firebrand from a funeral pyre, from chava, a corpse, and alata, a burning stick.

carryVoice: Your line: for self and others. The firebrand warms no one, inside or out. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 8 (Sallekha Sutta), the swamp image
